title: Counting Car Fleets Arriving at a Destination

phrases.explanation: To reach the same position as something ahead of you
A group of cars traveling together at the same speed
The duration needed to arrive at a destination
To start analyzing from the end toward the beginning
When a slower entity limits the speed of those behind it

technical_terms.definition: A group of one or more cars that travel at the speed of the slowest car because they cannot pass each other
A stack where elements are kept in strictly increasing or decreasing order
Arranging elements based on a specific attribute such as position
Calculated as the remaining distance divided by speed
Making locally optimal choices at each step to build a global solution

java_methods.description: Sorts a two-dimensional array, useful for sorting cars by position
Pushes an element onto the top of the stack
Returns the top element without removing it
Returns the number of elements in the stack

concept: Given an array of car positions and their speeds, all heading toward a common destination at a given target position, determine how many distinct car fleets will arrive at the destination. A car fleet is formed when a faster car catches up to a slower car ahead; they then travel together at the slower car's speed.

solutions.label: Brute Force Simulation
solutions.summary: Simulate each time step, moving all cars and merging them into fleets when they meet or overlap.

solutions.label: Sort and Compare Arrival Times
solutions.summary: Sort cars by position, compute each car's time to reach the target, and count how many distinct fleets form by comparing arrival times from the car closest to the target backward.

solutions.label: Stack-Based Fleet Counting
solutions.summary: Sort by position, then use a stack to track fleet leaders. Push arrival times and pop when a car merges into the fleet ahead.

sections.title: Understanding the Car Fleet Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Let's work on a problem. Imagine cars on a one-lane road, all heading toward the same destination. Each car has a starting position and a speed. Cars cannot pass each other. If a faster car catches a slower one, they form a fleet and travel at the slower speed. Given the target position, an array of positions, and an array of speeds, return the number of car fleets that arrive at the target.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Interesting. So if a car catches up to another before reaching the target, they merge into one fleet. Can positions be unsorted? And are all positions unique?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, positions can be given in any order, but every position is unique. Positions and speeds are positive integers. The array length can be up to ten thousand.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What if the array is empty or has one car?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: If empty, return zero. One car means one fleet. Let's use this example: target equals twelve, positions are ten, eight, zero, and speeds are two, four, one.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. Car A at ten with speed two takes one second. Car B at eight with speed four also takes one second, so B catches A and they form one fleet. Car C at zero with speed one takes twelve seconds and never catches up. So the answer is two fleets. Let me think about approaches.

sections.title: Brute Force Simulation
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style S0 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S1 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S2 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style R fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    S0["t=0: A=10, B=8, C=0"]
    S1["t=1: A=12 arrives, B=12 arrives, C=1"]
    S2["t=12: C=12 arrives"]
    R["Result: 2 fleets"]
    S0 --> S1
    S1 --> S2
    S2 --> R

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest idea is to simulate time step by step. At each step, move every car forward by its speed. If a car reaches or passes a car ahead, merge them into a fleet. Continue until all cars reach the target, then count the fleets.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time complexity of that approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: It's O of n times target in the worst case because we might simulate up to target time steps, and at each step we check all n cars. Space is O of n to store car states. This is too slow for large targets.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Right. Can you skip the simulation entirely?

sections.title: Sort and Compare Arrival Times
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style S1 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style S2 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style S3 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style S4 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style R fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    S1["Sort by position desc: A=10, B=8, C=0"]
    S2["Arrival times: A=1.0, B=1.0, C=12.0"]
    S3["A: new fleet, count=1. B: 1.0 <= 1.0, merges with A"]
    S4["C: 12.0 > 1.0, new fleet, count=2"]
    R["Answer: 2 fleets"]
    S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4 --> R

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Instead of simulating, I can calculate each car's arrival time directly as target minus position divided by speed. Then I sort cars by position in descending order, starting from the car closest to the target. I walk through the sorted list and track the current maximum arrival time. If a car's time exceeds the current max, it starts a new fleet.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Why does sorting by position and comparing times work?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: A car behind can only merge with the car directly ahead. If a behind car's arrival time is less than or equal to the car ahead, it catches up and merges. If its time is greater, it's too slow to catch up and forms a new fleet. By processing from front to back, we just compare against the current fleet leader's time.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good. The time complexity is O of n log n for sorting, and space is O of n. Can you formalize this with a stack?

sections.title: Stack-Based Fleet Counting
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style S1 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style S2 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style S3 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style S4 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style R fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    S1["Sort desc by position: A=10, B=8, C=0"]
    S2["Push A time=1.0 → Stack: [1.0]"]
    S3["B time=1.0 ≤ top 1.0 → skip. Stack: [1.0]"]
    S4["C time=12.0 > top 1.0 → push. Stack: [1.0, 12.0]"]
    R["Stack size = 2 fleets"]
    S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4 --> R

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I'll use a stack to make the logic cleaner. After sorting by position descending, I iterate through each car. I compute its arrival time. If the stack is empty or the time is greater than the top of the stack, I push it. Otherwise, the car merges with the fleet on top. The final stack size is the number of fleets.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk me through the example with the stack.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sorted by position descending: car A at ten, car B at eight, car C at zero. Push A's time one point zero. B's time is one point zero, not greater than the top, so skip it. C's time is twelve point zero, greater than the top, so push it. Stack has two elements, so the answer is two.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: The complexity is the same as the previous approach, O of n log n time and O of n space, but the stack gives a clean structure. Well done.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great job. You moved from a slow simulation to an efficient sort-and-compare solution, and then structured it neatly with a stack. The key insight is that calculating arrival times and processing cars from nearest to farthest lets us determine fleets without simulation.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Yes. The critical realization is that a car behind with a shorter arrival time will always merge into the fleet ahead. Sorting by position and using a stack makes this comparison straightforward. The stack naturally tracks fleet leaders.
